paragraphs: An online classifier ensemble combines several classifiers while training examples arrive over time. A central question is how much influence each classifier should have. This paper proposes updating probability distributions over those weights, so learning maintains a changing account of plausible weight settings as new observations arrive.

The framework connects Bayesian updating to the objective of minimizing prediction loss. For a specified class of loss functions, the authors construct a suitable likelihood, which makes the posterior distribution an approximation to the global empirical loss minimizer. This gives the probability-based updates a direct relationship to the ensemble’s training objective.

The convergence result depends on the data stream coming from a stationary process. Under that assumption, the framework achieves a better convergence rate toward the expected loss minimizer than standard stochastic gradient descent. Experiments on real datasets also show that it often beats online boosting. Together, these results support posterior-based weight estimation as both a theoretically motivated and empirically useful approach to online ensembles.
icml-2014-a-bayesian-framework-for-onlin.tldr: Bayesian updates to ensemble-weight distributions connect online classification to loss minimization and offer faster convergence under stationary data.

paragraphs: Semi-NMF compresses data into a lower-dimensional representation that can be interpreted in terms of clusters. The paper starts from the possibility that the relationship between those clusters and the original measurements contains several levels of hidden structure. A single clustering layer may not make these underlying attributes understandable.

Deep Semi-NMF introduces a layered model for learning such representations. Its purpose is to capture hidden attributes at different levels, allowing the resulting representations to be interpreted as groupings according to different, initially unknown properties of the data. The contribution therefore concerns both how data is compressed and what the compressed representation can express.

The authors report that the learned low-dimensional representations are better suited to clustering than those produced by Semi-NMF and other NMF variants. The stated finding supports using a hierarchy of representations when a single grouping does not capture the structure of interest. It connects the model’s ability to express hidden attributes with improved clustering performance.
icml-2014-a-deep-semi-nmf-model-for-lear.tldr: Deep Semi-NMF learns layered representations that capture hidden clustering attributes and improve clustering over the compared factorization methods.

paragraphs: In learning from experts, an algorithm repeatedly combines or selects advice and is evaluated against the best expert. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage of its decisions relative to that comparator. This paper develops an adaptive version of exponentiated gradient, using the optimistic learning framework to obtain more informative regret guarantees.

The new bounds depend on the variance and path length of the best expert. These quantities describe aspects of variability and change in the comparator’s losses, allowing the guarantee to reflect structure in the learning problem. The authors establish improvements over earlier results and resolve a previously posed open problem about this setting.

The approach also extends to matrix-valued losses, producing an adaptive matrix exponentiated gradient algorithm. To achieve the optimal regret bound in that case, the authors generalize Follow-the-Regularized-Leader to vector-valued payoffs. The contribution thus combines stronger expert-learning guarantees with a broader optimization construction that supports the matrix extension and may be useful independently.
icml-2014-adaptivity-and-optimism-an-imp.tldr: An adaptive exponentiated gradient method obtains stronger regret bounds tied to the best expert’s variability and extends to matrix-valued losses.

paragraphs: Many machine learning problems can be distributed by having several workers solve parts of a shared optimization problem and agree on a global solution. ADMM provides a way to coordinate that consensus. Its synchronized form, however, can spend substantial time waiting when some workers progress more slowly than others.

This paper introduces asynchronous ADMM with two controls on how independently workers may proceed: a partial barrier and bounded delay. These conditions constrain the asynchrony while allowing updates without full synchronization. The method therefore addresses waiting time through a controlled change to the coordination process, while retaining a simple algorithmic structure.

The authors provide convergence guarantees and relate the convergence rate to that of synchronous ADMM. Experiments across different distributed ADMM applications show reduced network waiting and faster convergence measured in elapsed wall-clock time. That distinction matters: the reported practical benefit concerns how quickly the distributed system reaches a solution, accounting for time spent coordinating its workers.
icml-2014-asynchronous-distributed-admm-.tldr: Controlled asynchronous ADMM reduces worker waiting and reaches solutions faster in the reported distributed experiments while retaining convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can benefit from identifying larger action units within demonstrated behavior. This paper treats the discovery of these macro-actions as a change-point detection problem: finding positions in a training sequence where one meaningful segment ends and another begins. The central challenge is learning those boundaries together with useful predictors.

The proposed supervised algorithm combines boosting with dynamic programming. It alternates between improving individual strong predictors and refining the estimated change-points. This links segmentation to discriminative learning, so the predictors and the division of the sequence are improved through the same overall process. The approach extends the classical boosting framework to accommodate uncertain boundaries.

The authors evaluate the method on classification tasks with naturally occurring change-points and then apply it to macro-action discovery in imitation learning. They demonstrate its use in complex image-based goal-planning problems involving thousands of features. These results show that the combined learning and segmentation procedure can support planning from rich visual inputs in the examined tasks.
icml-2014-dynamic-programming-boosting-f.tldr: Combining boosting with dynamic programming jointly improves predictors and sequence boundaries for discovering macro-actions in imitation learning.

paragraphs: Collective graphical models describe populations when observations are aggregate counts rather than records of individual behavior. They assume individuals are independent and identically distributed, but exact inference from the collective statistics is intractable. This paper develops a Gaussian approximation to make that inference more manageable.

The authors show that the collective distribution approaches a multivariate Gaussian as population size grows. The approximation preserves the original model’s conditional independence structure, retaining important relationships among its variables. When observations are exact marginals or are corrupted by Gaussian noise, inference in the approximation has an efficient closed-form solution.

Other observation models, including Poisson noise, are handled through expectation propagation, giving an additional approximate inference procedure. On a simulated bird migration problem, the authors compare the Gaussian approach with MCMC and MAP methods. It matches or improves on MAP accuracy while running significantly faster. The findings support the approximation as a practical route to population-level inference, with the inference procedure depending on how the counts are observed.
icml-2014-gaussian-approximation-of-coll.tldr: A Gaussian approximation preserves collective graphical models’ independence structure and enables fast inference from population counts.

paragraphs: Natural gradient ascent uses a metric tensor to shape optimization updates. Its usual formulation requires that metric to be positive definite. In applications, including those using the Fisher information matrix, the metric may only be positive semidefinite, leaving the standard method inapplicable in the form considered here.

The paper introduces generalized natural gradient ascent, or GeNGA, to accommodate positive semidefinite metrics that may also be nonsmooth. This extends the range of geometries the optimization method can handle. The authors then examine convergence rather than assuming that a natural-gradient construction automatically produces stable progress.

Their analysis shows that both ordinary natural gradient ascent and GeNGA can diverge in standard settings. They also establish sufficient conditions for several forms of convergence, separating the method’s definition from the conditions needed for successful optimization. Finally, they show how reinforcement learning methods that use natural gradients without positive definite metrics can be adapted to GeNGA. The result is both a broader algorithm and a more qualified understanding of its behavior.
icml-2014-genga-a-generalization-of-natu.tldr: GeNGA extends natural gradient ascent to semidefinite, nonsmooth metrics and establishes both divergence examples and sufficient convergence conditions.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of an expensive unknown function by modeling how that function behaves. Gaussian process models can struggle when the rate of variation changes across the input space. In hyperparameter optimization, practitioners often address this by manually changing coordinates, such as searching in logarithmic space.

This paper learns the coordinate transformation automatically. It uses the Beta cumulative distribution function to construct a broad family of bijective input warpings. Such transformations change how locations are represented while preserving a one-to-one correspondence with the original inputs, helping the model accommodate spatially varying length scales.

The authors also extend the framework to multiple tasks, allowing their input spaces to be warped into a jointly stationary representation. On challenging benchmark optimization tasks, adding warping produces better results more quickly and reliably than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support learning the search coordinates as part of the modeling process, especially when a fixed representation poorly captures how the objective changes.
icml-2014-input-warping-for-bayesian-opt.tldr: Automatically learned input transformations improve Bayesian optimization of nonstationary functions and extend to optimization across multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a target distribution concentrates on a strongly nonlinear region. A proposal that fits one part of that region may be poorly suited elsewhere. This paper introduces a Metropolis-Hastings sampler that adapts its proposals using information from the Markov chain’s previous trajectory.

The method represents that trajectory in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space and uses sample covariance there to inform new proposals. The feature-space moves can be integrated out analytically. Consequently, the actual proposal in the original space is Gaussian, with a mean and covariance that depend on the current location and reflect local covariance structure.

This construction requires no target gradients or higher-order information, making it attractive for settings such as pseudo-marginal MCMC. The authors describe it as computationally efficient and straightforward to implement. In synthetic and real-world examples with multivariate, highly nonlinear targets, it outperforms competing fixed and adaptive samplers. The results support adapting proposal geometry locally through kernels without requiring derivative information.
icml-2014-kernel-adaptive-metropolis-has.tldr: Kernel Adaptive Metropolis-Hastings learns location-dependent Gaussian proposals from past samples to explore nonlinear targets without gradients.

paragraphs: Superset label learning provides a set of possible labels for each training example, with the true label guaranteed to be somewhere in that set. A prediction counts as a superset error only when it falls outside the supplied set. This gives a usable training signal while leaving uncertainty about which included label is correct.

Many existing methods minimize this error to train a multiclass classifier. The paper asks when that strategy has a theoretical learning justification. It studies empirical risk minimization with superset error as the objective, connecting a common algorithmic choice to questions about learnability and the amount of training data required.

The analysis covers two ways such supervision can appear: independent instances and multiple-instance bags. For both, the authors establish conditions for empirical risk minimization to be learnable and provide sample-complexity results in the realizable case. That qualification is central to the contribution: the guarantees concern the stated setting where the learning problem is realizable, rather than unrestricted weakly labeled data.
icml-2014-learnability-of-the-superset-l.tldr: The paper establishes realizable-case learning conditions and sample complexity for classifiers trained by minimizing superset-label errors.

paragraphs: Deep networks can represent complex variation in data, but obtaining good performance often requires lengthy training. This paper proposes a technique called stretching, intended to improve the performance of the same models with very little training. It investigates stretching both as a mathematical construction and as a practical learning procedure.

For certain specific models, the authors show that learning remains tractable even when the weight matrix is stretched to infinity. They also develop tractable iterative algorithms for applying stretching to deep convolutional architectures and derive convergence bounds. These results connect an extreme version of the construction to algorithms that can actually be used.

Experiments suggest that stretched convolutional networks perform well on many object recognition tasks. The authors additionally report substantially better accuracy than backpropagation-based weight learning when the network architecture is held fixed. This comparison makes the learning procedure itself central to the finding: the reported gains arise within a fixed architecture, while the infinite-stretch tractability claim applies only to the specified models.
icml-2014-learning-by-stretching-deep-ne.tldr: Stretching offers a tractable alternative learning procedure that improves fixed-architecture deep-network accuracy in the reported object recognition experiments.

paragraphs: Large matrices in machine learning can contain hierarchical organization at several scales. The paper argues that traditional linear algebra tools, including eigendecomposition, may not capture all of this structure. It introduces multiresolution matrix factorization as a way to represent patterns that occur at different levels within the same matrix.

The construction draws on multiresolution analysis and produces a wavelet basis for sparse approximation. Its organizing idea is to make multiple scales part of the factorization itself. This matters when a useful matrix representation needs to describe both finer and broader structure, rather than treating hierarchical organization as incidental to the representation.

The authors identify two further uses for the factorization. It can compress matrices in a role similar to Nyström approximations, and it can serve as a prior for matrix completion. These uses connect the representation to reducing storage and expressing assumptions about missing entries. The contribution is a common multiscale framework that supports sparse approximation, compression, and completion.
icml-2014-multiresolution-matrix-factori.tldr: Multiresolution matrix factorization captures hierarchical matrix structure and supports sparse approximation, compression, and matrix-completion priors.

paragraphs: The paper studies principal components that must be both sparse and nonnegative for a positive semidefinite input matrix. These requirements constrain which components are allowed, making approximation quality an important concern. The proposed combinatorial algorithm searches a subspace determined by the matrix’s leading eigenvectors.

Its guarantees depend on the input spectrum: faster eigenvalue decay yields better approximation quality. When eigenvalues decay according to an asymptotically vanishing function, the algorithm can reach any requested accuracy with running time polynomial in matrix size and desired sparsity. The running time is not polynomial in inverse accuracy, so requesting greater precision has a distinct computational cost.

The authors also compute a dataset-specific bound by running an algorithm on the observed data. This bound is substantially tighter than the advance guarantees and certifies the reported proximity to the unknown optimum on every tested dataset. Empirically, the method matches or exceeds the compared state of the art. The contribution combines competitive solutions with evidence about their approximation quality.
icml-2014-nonnegative-sparse-pca-with-pr.tldr: A combinatorial algorithm for nonnegative sparse PCA provides spectrum-dependent guarantees and tighter dataset-specific certificates of approximation quality.

paragraphs: Training an object localizer usually requires knowing where objects appear, and producing those annotations is expensive. This paper learns localization from image-level labels that state only whether an object is present. The learning procedure must therefore discover useful object regions without being given their locations in the supervision.

The method combines two components. A discriminative submodular cover formulation automatically identifies a collection of positive object windows. A smoothed latent support vector machine then supplies the learning formulation, with smoothing allowing efficient quasi-Newton optimization. Together, these components connect the discovery of candidate regions with a tractable way to train the localization model.

On PASCAL VOC 2007 detection, the authors report a 50% relative improvement in mean average precision over the then-current state of the art. This is a relative gain, not an increase of 50 percentage points. The result demonstrates strong performance in the stated evaluation while using only object-presence labels, supporting the usefulness of combining region discovery with smooth latent-model optimization.
icml-2014-on-learning-to-localize-object.tldr: Learning object regions from image-presence labels yields a reported 50% relative mean-average-precision improvement on PASCAL VOC 2007 detection.

paragraphs: Online stochastic optimization with bandit feedback requires finding good inputs while observing rewards only for the choices made. This paper considers locally smooth objectives in a setting where reward observations can be correlated. Such dependence creates a challenge for existing methods that require rewards to be conditionally independent.

The proposed high-confidence tree algorithm, HCT, is an anytime method, meaning it can operate without a fixed stopping horizon. Its regret bounds match leading algorithms in their dependence on the number of steps and the near-optimality dimension. The contribution preserves those aspects of statistical performance while accommodating correlated feedback.

HCT also reduces memory requirements and uses a weaker smoothness assumption than existing anytime algorithms. These properties address storage and modeling demands alongside dependence between rewards. The authors discuss applying HCT to policy search in reinforcement learning and provide preliminary empirical results. That application illustrates the method’s potential use, while the main stated guarantees concern its regret behavior in the analyzed optimization setting.
icml-2014-online-stochastic-optimization.tldr: HCT handles correlated bandit rewards with competitive regret bounds, lower memory needs, and weaker smoothness requirements than existing anytime methods.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering learns preferences from observed user ratings, but the ratings that appear may be a selective sample. Users might rate items they like more often than items they dislike. In that situation, treating missing ratings as missing at random can bias inference and harm predictions.

This paper proposes a probabilistic matrix factorization model that learns two processes together: how ratings are generated and how they become observed. The missingness mechanism is therefore part of the model, allowing the learning procedure to account for a relationship between preferences and rating availability. The authors present this as a viable matrix factorization approach for data missing not at random.

Joint learning improves both rating prediction and modeling of the observation process relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. These findings support treating selective observation as part of the recommendation problem itself. The authors regard the results as promising and anticipate further gains from future work on such models; those anticipated gains are an expectation rather than an established experimental result.
icml-2014-probabilistic-matrix-factoriza.tldr: Jointly modeling ratings and their selective observation improves collaborative filtering when data is missing not at random.

paragraphs: Tracking expert advice becomes more complicated when every decision changes the learner’s state. This paper studies a setting where both the learner and experts make local moves through a continuous, bounded region. Payoffs depend on each participant’s current position and action, so past decisions affect the circumstances of later choices.

The formulation connects online expert learning with the stateful structure of reinforcement learning. Standard no-regret methods no longer apply directly. The authors combine online learning techniques with pursuit-evasion results to construct a simple algorithm that provably achieves no regret when the state space is a convex Euclidean region.

A trading application gives the geometry a concrete interpretation: the allowed region represents inventory-risk constraints, and local moves limit market impact. Experiments using historical market data show a strong advantage over classic no-regret approaches. The result supports accounting for state and movement constraints when learning from experts, with the theoretical guarantee tied to the stated convex state-space setting.
icml-2014-pursuit-evasion-without-regret.tldr: A pursuit-evasion-inspired algorithm achieves no regret for stateful expert tracking in convex regions and shows advantages on historical trading data.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix is useful across many applications, but existing methods can deteriorate when matrices are large or ill-conditioned. This paper proposes Riemannian Pursuit to address both difficulties together. The approach organizes recovery as a sequence of optimization problems with progressively increasing rank.

Each stage fixes the rank and uses a nonlinear Riemannian conjugate gradient method to improve the current solution. The correction focuses on an important subspace whose size increases over the sequence. This makes recovery a process of refining a constrained representation and then expanding the space in which further improvements can be made.

The authors prove linear convergence under conditions they describe as mild. They also report substantial experimental improvements over existing methods on large-scale and ill-conditioned matrices. The theoretical result concerns the rate of progress under its conditions, while the experiments demonstrate the method’s practical behavior on the difficult matrix settings that motivated it. Together, they support combining fixed-rank refinement with progressive subspace expansion.
icml-2014-riemannian-pursuit-for-big-mat.tldr: Riemannian Pursuit progressively expands fixed-rank optimization subproblems to recover large and ill-conditioned matrices efficiently.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference on massive datasets can benefit from processing smaller subsets, but combining the resulting analyses is a central challenge. The paper seeks a general approach that supports distributed computation while remaining robust to corrupted observations. Its motivation includes the problem-specific and ad hoc nature of many existing distributed Bayesian techniques.

The method divides the observations into non-overlapping subgroups and computes a posterior distribution from each independent subgroup. It then combines those distributions using their geometric median. This aggregation step is the main novelty: the procedure operates on the subgroup posterior distributions themselves to form the combined result.

Splitting the data addresses computational scale, while the median-based aggregation provides the basis for robustness to corruption. The authors present theoretical and numerical results illustrating the approach’s advantages. The contribution is therefore a general pattern for distributed Bayesian inference in which the choice of aggregation is integral to reliability, connecting smaller independent analyses to a combined posterior-based summary.
icml-2014-scalable-and-robust-bayesian-i.tldr: Combining subgroup posterior distributions through a geometric median provides a scalable Bayesian inference approach robust to data corruption.

paragraphs: Sequence tagging requires predicting related outputs across a sequence, and latent-variable structured models can represent hidden relationships involved in those predictions. This paper develops a convex optimization formulation for training such models with a max-margin objective. The formulation makes the representation used to score input-output relationships central to the learning problem.

The scores come from input-output observable operator models. The authors express learning through an optimization problem involving a low-rank Hankel matrix that represents the operator model. This matrix view creates a direct connection between the structured predictor and a representation whose rank is part of the formulation.

The resulting contribution is a spectral regularization method for max-margin structured prediction. Its purpose is to control model capacity: how much complexity the predictor can express during learning. Experiments confirm that the proposed regularization framework provides an effective way to exercise that control. The paper therefore links a convex training formulation, an operator-based scoring model, and matrix-based regularization within one approach.
icml-2014-spectral-regularization-for-ma.tldr: A convex operator-model formulation yields spectral regularization that effectively controls capacity in max-margin structured prediction.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses gradient-driven dynamics to propose distant moves with high acceptance probabilities, helping it explore more efficiently than ordinary random-walk proposals. Computing those gradients becomes impractical with very large or streaming datasets. Using a data subset offers a cheaper gradient estimate, but introduces noise into the dynamics.

The paper shows that directly substituting noisy gradients into HMC can behave arbitrarily badly. It introduces a variant based on second-order Langevin dynamics with a friction term that counteracts the gradient noise. The resulting construction maintains the desired target distribution as an invariant distribution, addressing the statistical consequences of the approximation.

Simulated-data experiments validate the theory, and the authors apply the method to neural-network classification and online Bayesian matrix factorization. The contribution explains why computational savings from subset gradients require a corresponding change in the sampling dynamics. Its central result is a way to incorporate that noise while preserving the intended distribution, together with demonstrations in two learning applications.
icml-2014-stochastic-gradient-hamiltonia.tldr: Stochastic gradient HMC adds friction to counteract noisy gradients and preserve the desired target distribution.

paragraphs: Recurrent temporal restricted Boltzmann machines model short- and long-term dependencies in time series. Their fully connected visible-hidden structure, however, does not explicitly reflect the dependency pattern among observations. This paper proposes learning and using that structure to support prediction and reveal relationships within the data.

The structured RTRBM incorporates a dependency graph into both the model structure and its energy function. The approach is related to graphical lasso methods for learning Gaussian graphical-model topology. The authors also develop a spike-and-slab RTRBM and combine it with structure learning to accommodate datasets whose observations are real valued.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the structured model can improve prediction over the original RTRBM, especially when there are many visible units but relatively few training examples. It also reveals structure in the benchmark datasets. These findings support explicitly modeling dependencies as a useful source of both predictive information and interpretable patterns, with the strongest reported benefits arising in the stated data regime.
icml-2014-structured-recurrent-temporal-.tldr: Structured RTRBMs learn dependency graphs that can improve time-series prediction and reveal underlying relationships, particularly with many variables and limited training data.

paragraphs: In a contextual bandit problem, a learner observes a context, chooses one of several actions, and receives feedback only for the chosen action. It must learn good decisions from this incomplete information. This paper develops an algorithm that combines a statistically optimal regret guarantee with a low number of calls to a supervised-learning oracle.

The oracle solves fully supervised cost-sensitive classification problems. Assuming access to that capability, the algorithm needs only approximately the square root of K times T oracle calls across T rounds, with logarithmic factors suppressed, where K is the number of actions. This connects contextual bandit learning to an existing supervised optimization primitive.

The reduced oracle-call requirement is the basis for the authors’ practicality claim among approaches supporting general policy classes. A proof-of-concept experiment evaluates an online variant and shows strong computational and statistical performance against several strong baselines. The result combines an optimal theoretical regret guarantee under the oracle assumption with an initial empirical demonstration of computational usefulness.
icml-2014-taming-the-monster-a-fast-and-.tldr: A contextual bandit algorithm achieves statistically optimal regret using roughly √(KT) supervised cost-sensitive classification oracle calls, up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: A neighborhood graph reflects both relationships among sampled points and the density from which those points were drawn. This paper asks how to study such a graph as though its points had instead come from another density. The proposed solution changes edge weights to adjust the graph’s cuts and volumes.

The authors introduce the f-adjusted graph and prove that its cuts and volumes approach the desired alternatives as sample size grows without bound. They also give an algebraic interpretation: the adjusted normalized Laplacian belongs to a natural family of diagonal modifications of the original normalized Laplacian. This connects a geometric change of sampling density to a matrix operation.

Algorithms based on cuts and volumes, including spectral clustering, can then operate on the adjusted graph. The method offers a way to investigate an alternative sampling distribution without access to a new sample from it. The authors identify sample-bias correction, data uniformization, and multiscale graph analysis as applications, with the correctness guarantee stated in the large-sample limit.
icml-2014-the-f-adjusted-graph-laplacian.tldr: Reweighting a neighborhood graph makes its cuts and volumes asymptotically behave as if the data came from a different density.

paragraphs: Graph clustering often relies on observations of whether pairs of nodes are connected, but those observations may have unequal reliability. This paper gives more weight to lower-uncertainty observations and formulates clustering as an efficiently solvable convex optimization problem. Both observed edges and observed absences can carry different confidence levels.

Under a generative model, the authors establish recovery guarantees through a theorem covering arbitrary choices of weights and uncertainty distributions. Optimizing the weights produces a provably optimal scheme that matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. This connects confidence weighting to formal limits on recovering the underlying clusters.

The analysis also shows that unequal uncertainty can be beneficial. In the studied resource-allocation setting, concentrating measurement resources to obtain accurate observations for a few node pairs is preferable to spreading them across many inaccurate observations. Simulations validate the theoretical findings. The contribution therefore informs both how to cluster an existing uncertain graph and how to allocate resources when collecting its measurements.
icml-2014-weighted-graph-clustering-with.tldr: Confidence-weighted convex graph clustering achieves strong recovery guarantees and shows that concentrating measurement accuracy can improve clustering.
